planting.note: Set divisions in full sun on well-drained soil; this early red earns its Lenington award by holding bloom quality across widely different climates.

directions: Hybridized by Laura Pearl Hancock and registered in 1960, Skiatook Cardinal took the Lenington All-American Award in 1972 for its dependable scarlet-red blooms with recurved petals and a small green throat. It is one of the earliest-flowering reds in commerce, opening well before most other cultivars start their season. Clumps multiply readily and tolerate a wide range of soils and climates with minimal care. Divide every three to four years to keep bloom counts high and foliage vigorous.

planting.note: Grow in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; dormant foliage benefits from a season-end cleanup in colder zones.

directions: Registered in 1968 by Hubert A. Fischer, Oriental Ruby won the Lenington All-American Award in 1979 for its carmine-red self blooms with a small green throat held above dormant foliage. Mid-to-late season flowering extends the garden's red color range after earlier reds have finished. Established clumps are vigorous growers that perform reliably across a broad range of soils and climates. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to renew flowering.

planting.note: Plant along border edges or in small containers; this compact, lightly fragrant diploid stays low and multiplies quickly.

directions: Hybridized by Kennedy and registered in 1972, Raindrop earned the Lenington All-American Award in 1982 after also taking the Donn Fischer Memorial Cup and an Award of Merit. Its light-yellow, slightly fragrant blooms are small and numerous atop compact, semi-evergreen foliage well suited to edging beds. The diminutive habit makes it a dependable choice for small gardens and mixed borders alike. Divide clumps every two to three years to maintain a tidy, floriferous mound.

planting.note: Site in full sun with moderate, even moisture; semi-evergreen foliage benefits from mulch protection in colder winters.

directions: Registered in 1974 by Pittard, Red Rum received the Annie T. Giles Award in 1979 before going on to win the Lenington All-American Award in 1984 for its rusty-red self blooms with a contrasting yellow throat. The compact midseason bloomer stays low and dense, making it useful as a long-lived front-of-border plant. Semi-evergreen foliage holds up well through mild winters and rebounds quickly each spring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to sustain bloom production.

planting.note: Grow in full sun with consistent moisture; evergreen foliage and heat tolerance make this a strong choice for southern gardens.

directions: Hybridized by W. Spalding and introduced in 1976, Yesterday Memories collected an Award of Merit in 1985 and the Lenington All-American Award in 1986 on the strength of its deep-pink, green-throated blooms held on sturdy evergreen scapes. Extended daily bloom time and strong heat tolerance give it an unusually long season of color. It performs reliably in both humid southern summers and cooler northern gardens alike. Divide every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant in full sun and fertile soil; dormant foliage and a tetraploid constitution give this cultivar strong cold hardiness.

directions: Hybridized by Peck and registered in 1968, Golden Prize earned the Lenington All-American Award in 1987 for its large gold self blooms produced late in the season when many other daylilies have finished flowering. The tetraploid habit gives the plant sturdy scapes and heavier-textured petals that hold up well in heat and rain. Dormant foliage dies back cleanly in autumn and returns reliably each spring across cold climates. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Beauty to Behold Daylily (Lenington All-American Winner)

planting.note: Site in full sun with well-drained soil; semi-evergreen foliage and vigorous increase make this a reliable mass-planting daylily.

directions: Registered by Sellers in 1978, Beauty to Behold won the Lenington All-American Award in 1993 for its clear lemon self blooms held on sturdy, midseason scapes. The semi-evergreen diploid multiplies quickly, forming dense, floriferous clumps within a few seasons of planting. Its wide geographic adaptability has made it a dependable garden performer from northern to southern climates. Divide every three to four years to prevent overcrowding and sustain peak bloom.

planting.note: Grow in full sun with even moisture; tall scapes and huge unusual-form blooms benefit from staking in windy sites.

directions: Hybridized by Joiner and registered in 1991, Jan's Twister received an Award of Merit in 1997 and the Lambert/Webster Award in 2000 before winning the Lenington All-American Award in 2003. Its huge peach petals twist, curl, and fold unpredictably so that no two flowers open quite alike, a hallmark of its unusual-form class. The evergreen diploid reblooms over a long early-to-midseason window given adequate moisture. Divide established clumps every three to four years to keep the oversized blooms coming.

common_name: Margo Reed Indeed Daylily (Lenington All-American Winner)

planting.note: Plant in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil; the broad ruffled edge and chartreuse throat show best with consistent watering.

directions: Bred by J.P. Murphy from After Awhile Crocodile crossed with Loch Ness Monster and registered in 2004, Margo Reed Indeed built a rare award sweep: Honorable Mention in 2007, Award of Merit in 2010, the Lambert/Webster Award in 2011, and the Lenington All-American Award in 2016. Its large cream-white blooms carry soft pink undertones and a ruffled white edge framing a chartreuse throat. The cultivar's broad regional adaptability was the deciding factor in its Lenington win. Divide clumps every three to four years to maintain strong bloom scapes.
